batchName: Late Republic: Caesar in Gaul (58-50 BCE) - Easy Batch 2
chapterName: Late Republic: Caesar in Gaul (58-50 BCE)

questions.question: Why is the Gallic side of the war's story lost?
options: Druid texts perished in a fire
questions.explanation: With no Gallic histories, we depend almost entirely on Caesar's version. Since the Second World War, scholars have grown sceptical of it.
questions.sourceQuote: The Gauls wrote no histories, so their side of the story is lost.

questions.question: Why did Caesar build a second, outer ring of fortifications at Alesia?
options: To mark the new province's border
To face the Gallic relief army
questions.explanation: The inner ring penned the Gauls in, while the outer ring, about 21 km long, faced outward against the relievers.
questions.sourceQuote: An outer ring about 21 km (14 Roman miles) long faced outward against the relievers.

questions.question: Where does almost all our knowledge of the Gallic War come from?
questions.explanation: Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic War reached Rome in instalments, keeping his exploits before the public. Its plain Latin still makes it a classic school text.
questions.sourceQuote: Almost everything known about the war comes from Julius Caesar himself.

questions.question: At which town did Vercingetorix inflict a clear defeat on Caesar in 52 BC?
questions.explanation: At Gergovia Caesar admitted 700 dead, including 46 centurions. Historians suspect the real losses were much higher.
questions.sourceQuote: At Gergovia, Vercingetorix inflicted a clear defeat.

questions.question: Vercingetorix was a nobleman of which powerful tribe of central Gaul?
questions.explanation: He was born around 82 BC at Gergovia, chief town of the Arverni. Later, at Gergovia, he would hand Caesar a clear defeat.
questions.sourceQuote: Vercingetorix was born around 82 BC at Gergovia, chief town of the Arverni, a powerful tribe of central Gaul.

questions.question: What was the Roman army's great weak point during the Gallic War?
questions.explanation: Each soldier carried only a few days' rations, so food was a constant worry. Again and again, hunger dictated Caesar's moves.

questions.question: How many cohorts made up a Roman legion in Caesar's day?
questions.explanation: A legion of around 5,000 men was split into ten cohorts of 480 soldiers each. The cohort had replaced the smaller maniple.
questions.sourceQuote: Each legion was split into ten cohorts (*cohortes*) of 480 soldiers.

questions.question: What was Vercingetorix's ultimate fate?
options: Pardoned and made a Roman ally
Paraded in a triumph and strangled
Killed in the fighting at Alesia
questions.explanation: After about six years in captivity, he was paraded in Caesar's triumph in 46 BC and strangled in the Tullianum. Since the 19th century he has been a French national hero.
questions.sourceQuote: In 46 BC he was paraded in Caesar's triumph and then strangled in the Tullianum, Rome's prison.

questions.question: Which two men shared power with Julius Caesar in the informal pact later called the First Triumvirate?
questions.explanation: Caesar's partners were Pompey, Rome's most celebrated general, and Crassus, its richest man. Their backing won Caesar his governorship in Gaul.
questions.sourceQuote: His partners were Pompey, Rome's most celebrated general, and Crassus, its richest man.

questions.question: Why did Caesar scatter his legions' winter camps across Gaul in 54 BC?
options: To guard every river crossing in Gaul
To prepare a second invasion of Britain
To stop the legions mutinying together
To spread the burden of feeding them after failed harvests
questions.explanation: Harvests had failed, yet Caesar made the tribes feed his legions over winter. Scattering the camps spread the burden but left each one isolated.
questions.sourceQuote: To spread the burden he scattered their camps, which left each one isolated.
